# Joins and `dplyr` practice

## Dataset 1

We start by making some "healthcare" data: 

```{r}
library(tidyverse) ## add this line! (and fix line 98)
# Patients table
patients <- tibble(
  patient_id = c(1, 2, 3, 4),
  name = c("Alice", "Bob", "Charlie", "David"),
  age = c(25, 40, 35, 50),
  sex = c("F", "M", "F", "M")
)

# Visits table (Some patients have multiple visits, some missing)
visits <- tibble(
  visit_id = c(101, 102, 103, 104, 105),
  patient_id = c(1, 2, 2, 3, 5),  
  doctor_id = c(201, 202, 201, 203, 204),
  visit_date = as.Date(c("2024-01-10", "2024-01-12", "2024-02-15", "2024-03-01", "2024-03-10"))
)

# Doctors table (Some doctors may not have treated any patients)
doctors <- tibble(
  doctor_id = c(201, 202, 203, 205),
  doctor_name = c("Dr. Smith", "Dr. Johnson", "Dr. Lee", "Dr. Brown"),
  specialty = c("Cardiology", "Neurology", "Pediatrics", "Orthopedics")
)

```

Questions: 

- Find the names of patients who have visited the hospital. 
- Show all patients visit information, even if they haven't visited the hospital
- List all the visits and patient information, even if there isn't information for the patient
- Show all visits with their assigned doctors.
- Find the doctor(s) that Bob has met with. 
- Find patients that haven't visited the hospital

```{r}
# - Find the names of patients who have visited the hospital. 
semi_join(patients, visits) |> select(name)

# - Show all patients' visit information, even if they haven't visited the hospital
left_join(patients, visits) 

# - List all the visits with their patient information, even if there isn't information for the patient
left_join(visits, patients)
## or 
right_join(patients, visits)

# - Show all visits with their assigned doctors.
left_join(visits, doctors, join_by(doctor_id)) ## do I need this join_by? no. 

# - Find the doctor(s) that Bob has met with. 
## this one needs two joins! 
## how do I get this!? I need Bob's name, his visits, and the doctors for each visit. 
left_join(patients, visits) |> 
  filter(name == "Bob") |>  ## take the result and filter to only Bob
  left_join(doctors) |>  ## join this new "only bob visits" data with the matching doctors
  select(doctor_name)  ## only show the doctor vector

# - Find patients that haven't visited the hospital
anti_join(patients, visits)

```

## Dataset 2

Load the `"nycflights13"` package.  You'll also need to load `dplyr` or `tidyverse`, if you didn't above.

```{r}
library(tidyverse)
#install.packages("nycflights13")
library(nycflights13)
my_flights <- flights # store my own version
my_flights <- na.omit(my_flights) 
  ## this dataset has data on cancelled flights too, 
  ## so we 'll remove those for now

```


Create a dataframe of the average arrival delays for each _destination_

```{r}
avg_arr_delay_df <- my_flights |> 
  group_by(dest) |> 
  summarise(avg_arr_delay = mean(arr_delay)) |> 
  arrange(-avg_arr_delay)
```

Then use `left_join()` to join on the "airports" dataframe, which has the airport information.

```{r}
data("airports") # this will put the data in your environment (optional)
left_join(avg_arr_delay_df, airports, join_by(dest == faa)) |> select(avg_arr_delay, name)
```
Note here: the column names don't match anymore! 

Which airport had the largest average arrival delay?

```{r}
left_join(avg_arr_delay_df, airports, join_by(dest == faa)) |> 
  select(avg_arr_delay, name) |> 
  slice_max(avg_arr_delay)
```



What is the average departure delay for each airline? To answer this with something more than just the FAA code of the airline name, you need to create a dataframe of the average departure delay for each _airline_, then use `left_join()` to join on the "airlines" dataframe


```{r}
my_flights |> 
  summarise(avg_dep_delay = mean(dep_delay), 
            .by = carrier) |> 
  left_join(airlines) |>  
  select(name, avg_dep_delay)



## get rid of one of the tick marks below - should be 3
``` 

Which airline had the smallest average departure delay? 



```{r}
my_flights |> 
  summarise(avg_dep_delay = mean(dep_delay), 
            .by = carrier) |> 
  left_join(airlines) |>  
  select(name, avg_dep_delay) |> 
  arrange(avg_dep_delay)

## OR 

my_flights |> 
  summarise(avg_dep_delay = mean(dep_delay), 
            .by = carrier) |> 
  left_join(airlines) |>  
  select(name, avg_dep_delay) |> 
  slice_min(avg_dep_delay)


```


Add origin and destination airport names (two joins to the same table)
Question: Which origin–destination pair has the highest average arrival delay?


```{r}
my_flights |> 
  left_join(airports, join_by(origin == faa)) |> 
  left_join(airports, join_by(dest == faa), suffix = c("_origin", "_dest")) 
    ## we can add this suffix to make it clear which columns are for the origin (from the first join) and which are from the destination (from the second join)

my_flights |> 
  left_join(airports, join_by(origin == faa)) |> 
  left_join(airports, join_by(dest == faa), suffix = c("_origin", "_dest")) |> 
  summarise(mean_arr_delay = mean(arr_delay),
            n_flights = n(),
            .by = c(name_origin, name_dest)) |> 
    ## grouping by the new names so that they stick around
  arrange(-mean_arr_delay) |> 
  select(mean_arr_delay, n_flights, name_origin, name_dest)
``` 

Which airline (name) has the highest on-time rate? Are left_join and inner_join returning the same rows here? Why?


```{r}
my_flights |> 
  left_join(airlines) |> 
  mutate(on_time = arr_delay <= 5) |> 
  summarise(on_time_count = sum(on_time), 
            flight_count = n(), 
            on_time_perc = on_time_count / flight_count * 100,
            .by = name) |> 
  slice_max(on_time_perc, n = 4)
  


dim(my_flights |> left_join(airlines)) == dim(my_flights |> inner_join(airlines))
## same number of rows and columns - this tells us that there isn't a carrier in the data that's missing in the lookup table

```

Plane metadata join: age of aircraft vs. delays
Among aircraft with at least 50 flights, which tailnumber has the largest average arrival delay, and what are the manufacturer/model and age?


```{r}
my_flights |> 
  left_join(planes, join_by(tailnum)) |> 
  add_count(tailnum, name = "n_flights_of_plane") |> 
    ## counts the flights for each plane, adds it as a column! 
  filter(n_flights_of_plane >= 50) |> 
  summarise(avg_arr_delay = mean(arr_delay), 
            .by = c(tailnum, manufacturer, year.y)) |> 
  arrange(-avg_arr_delay)


my_flights |> 
  left_join(planes, join_by(tailnum)) |> 
  add_count(tailnum, name = "n_flights_of_plane") |> 
    ## counts the flights for each plane, adds it as a column! 
  filter(n_flights_of_plane >= 50) |> 
  summarise(avg_arr_delay = mean(arr_delay), 
            .by = c(tailnum, manufacturer, year.y)) |> 
  drop_na(year.y) |>
  mutate(man_simp = fct_lump_n(manufacturer, n = 6)) |> 
  ggplot(aes(x = year.y, y = avg_arr_delay)) + 
  geom_density_2d_filled() + 
  facet_wrap(~ man_simp) + 
  theme(legend.position = "none")

```

## Extra Examples from R4DS:    

```{r}

top_dest <- flights %>%
  count(dest, sort = TRUE) %>%
  head(10)
top_dest

```

Now you want to find each flight that went to one of those destinations. You could, of course, filter. But! Now you can semi-join: 

```{r}
flights %>% 
  semi_join(top_dest)
```


What does anti_join(flights, airports, by = c("dest" = "faa")) tell you? What does anti_join(airports, flights, by = c("faa" = "dest")) tell you?
Perform the two joins below and consider what the results **are**. 

```{r}
anti_join(flights, airports, by = c("dest" = "faa"))
## these are the flights going to airports that aren't in the "airports" lookup table

anti_join(airports, flights, by = c("faa" = "dest"))
## these are the airports in the lookup table that are not the destination of flights from NYC
```
